headline: Guatemala: Mayan Roots to Modern Struggles
tldr: A rapid tour of Guatemala's geography, Mayan glory, colonial conquest, civil war, and the culture that survived it all.

mindmap.label: Guatemala
mindmap.note: A tour of Guatemala's geography, Mayan history, culture, and economy as a country shaped by its ancient civilization.

children.label: Geography
children.note: Guatemala sits in Central America bordering Mexico, Belize, Honduras and El Salvador, split into four distinct regions.

children.label: Pacific Coastal Plain
children.note: Runs along the Pacific Ocean and holds Guatemala City, the country's largest city.

children.label: Northern Highlands
children.note: Stretch from Mexico south through central Guatemala, full of volcanoes and mountains.

children.label: Peten Region
children.note: Northern lowland rainforests containing many Mayan archaeological sites.

children.label: Eastern Highlands
children.note: Borders Honduras and contains Lake Isabal, Guatemala's largest lake.

children.label: Three mountain chains
children.note: The Sierra Madre runs along the Pacific coast; the Kuchumatanes and Chacas ranges run parallel through central Guatemala.

children.label: Tropical climate
children.note: Lowlands are hot and humid, highlands are cooler, with a wet season from May to October prone to tropical storms.

children.label: Lakes and rivers
children.note: Lake Isabal covers over 565 sq km, Lake Atitlan is a deep crater lake ringed by volcanoes, and the Motagua River is the longest, bordering Honduras.

children.label: Ancient Mayan civilization
children.note: The Mayan civilization began around 2,000 BC and peaked in the classic period, leaving behind cities, writing, and science.

children.label: Rise and peak
children.note: Development began around 2,000 BC and reached its height in the classic period, 250 AD to 900 AD.

children.label: City-states
children.note: Major sites like Tikal, El Mirador and Kaminaljuyu featured step pyramids, palaces, temples, observatories and ball courts.

children.label: Writing and the Popol Vuh
children.note: A complex hieroglyphic writing system produced texts including the creation story the Popol Vuh.

children.label: Science and math
children.note: Mayans advanced art, architecture, astronomy and calendar systems, and their math used the concept of zero and large numbers.

children.label: Decline and continuity
children.note: The southern lowlands declined around 900 AD, but northern Mayans thrived into the post-classic period until the Spanish conquest.

children.label: Legacy today
children.note: Visible in archaeological sites, architecture and Mayan descendants who still keep ancient traditions alive.

children.label: Colonial era and independence
children.note: Spanish conquest reshaped Guatemala, followed by a long, unsteady path to full independence.

children.label: Spanish conquest
children.note: Spain arrived in the early 1500s, conquered the Mayans, and ruled as the Captaincy General of Guatemala.

children.label: Cultural destruction
children.note: The Spanish destroyed many Mayan texts and forced conversion to Christianity, sparking some Mayan uprisings.

children.label: Path to independence
children.note: Guatemala gained independence in 1821, briefly joined the first Mexican Empire, then the Federal Republic of Central America, before becoming fully independent in 1839.

children.label: 20th-century turmoil
children.note: A century of dictatorship, brief democracy, a US-backed coup, and a brutal 36-year civil war.

children.label: Dictatorships and United Fruit
children.note: From the late 19th century to 1944, dictators ruled closely allied with the United Fruit Company and the United States.

children.label: Democratic decade
children.note: A democratic government ruled from 1945 to 1954, ending in a US-backed coup.

children.label: 36-year civil war
children.note: Leftist rebels fought military regimes; indigenous Mayans were targeted by the military during the conflict.

children.label: War's end and recovery
children.note: The civil war ended in 1996; Guatemala has since worked to rebuild but still faces poverty, inequality and corruption.

children.label: People and religion
children.note: A majority-indigenous population practices a blend of Catholic and Mayan spiritual traditions.

children.label: Ethnic makeup
children.note: Indigenous Mayans are 40-60% of the population, largest group the K'iche', followed by Kaqchikel, Mam, Q'eqchi' and others, each with its own language and customs.

children.label: Mestizo population
children.note: About 40% of Guatemalans are mestizo, a mix of European and indigenous ancestry, plus small European, African, Asian and Middle Eastern minorities.

children.label: Religious blend
children.note: 50-60% are Catholic and 40% Protestant, but Mayan people often blend Catholic practice with indigenous beliefs tied to nature, ancestors and the Mayan calendar.

children.label: Language
children.note: Spanish is official, but the government recognizes 23 indigenous languages alongside it.

children.label: Over 20 Mayan languages
children.note: Main ones include K'iche', Kaqchikel and Mam; many Mayans are monolingual in their native language.

children.label: Economy
children.note: An agricultural economy worth about $95 billion, leaning on coffee and bananas but held back by inequality.

children.label: Agricultural exports
children.note: Guatemala is one of the world's largest exporters of coffee and bananas, plus sugar, corn, beans, cardamom and vegetables.

children.label: Manufacturing and tourism
children.note: Food processing, clothing, furniture and pharmaceuticals lead manufacturing; tourism centers on natural beauty and Mayan sites.

children.label: Inequality and poverty
children.note: GDP per capita is around $8,200, yet over 50% of the population lives below the poverty line amid low tax revenue and corruption.

children.label: Trade with the US
children.note: The United States takes over a third of Guatemala's exports and supplies a quarter of its imports.

children.label: Arts and literature
children.note: Guatemalan literature and art fuse Mayan roots with Spanish colonial influence, producing a Nobel laureate.

children.label: Literary tradition
children.note: Began with Mayan hieroglyphic writing and the Popol Vuh; later writers include Jose Mila, Rafael Spinola, and Nobel laureate Miguel Angel Asturias.

children.label: Visual and fabric arts
children.note: Painter Andres Curruchich is known for depicting Mayan life; weavers use bright colors and patterns like the traditional huipil blouse.

children.label: Music
children.note: Marimbas, maracas, chirimias, flutes and wooden drums remain central to Guatemalan culture.

children.label: Cuisine
children.note: A mix of Mayan staples and Spanish influence built around corn, beans, and hearty stews.

children.label: Staples
children.note: Corn, beans, chili peppers and rice form the dietary base of Guatemalan food.

children.label: Tostadas
children.note: A fried corn tortilla topped with tomato sauce, cabbage, lettuce, meat and cheese, garnished with avocado or radish.

children.label: Tamales
children.note: Made from masa stuffed with seasoned meat, vegetables or cheese, wrapped in banana leaves or corn husks and steamed.

children.label: Pache de pollo
children.note: A traditional chicken soup with ham, rice, vegetables and herbs, likely influenced by Spanish cocido and taking hours to prepare.

children.label: Jocon
children.note: An iconic meat stew layered with plantains, potatoes, tomatoes, peppers and herbs; the name comes from the Mayan word for sauce.

events.label: Ancient Mayan civilization begins
events.detail: The Mayan civilization started developing in what is now Guatemala.

events.label: Classic period peak
events.detail: The Mayans reached their peak, building city-states like Tikal, El Mirador and Kaminaljuyu.

events.label: Southern lowlands decline
events.detail: The southern Mayan lowlands declined while northern Mayans continued into the post-classic period.

events.label: Spanish conquest begins
events.detail: The Spanish arrived and conquered the Mayans and other indigenous peoples, later ruling as the Captaincy General of Guatemala.

events.label: Guatemala gains independence
events.detail: Guatemala became independent, briefly joining the first Mexican Empire and then the Federal Republic of Central America.

events.label: Full independence achieved
events.detail: Guatemala became fully independent, followed by political instability between liberals and conservatives.

events.label: Dictators allied with United Fruit
events.detail: A series of dictators ruled Guatemala closely allied to the United Fruit Company and the United States.

events.label: Democratic government rules
events.detail: A democratic government governed until it was toppled by a US-backed coup in 1954.

events.label: 36-year civil war
events.detail: Leftist rebels fought military regimes while indigenous Mayans were targeted by the military.

events.label: Civil war ends
events.detail: The war ended and Guatemala began rebuilding, though poverty, inequality and corruption persisted.

summary: This documentary frames Guatemala through the lens of its ancient Mayan roots, tracing the civilization from its origins around 2,000 BC through its architectural and intellectual peak in the classic period, when city-states like Tikal and El Mirador built pyramids and developed writing, math, and astronomy. It shows how that world declined in the south but persisted in the north until the Spanish arrived.

The video then moves through Guatemala's colonial and modern political history: Spanish conquest in the early 1500s, a bumpy road to full independence by 1839, decades of dictatorship tied to the United Fruit Company, a brief democratic window from 1945-1954 ended by a US-backed coup, and a brutal 36-year civil war that specifically targeted indigenous Mayans before ending in 1996.

Culturally, the film paints Guatemala as majority indigenous, with Mayans making up 40-60% of the population and speaking over 20 distinct languages, while religion blends Catholic and Protestant practice with indigenous spiritual traditions tied to nature and the Mayan calendar.

Economically, Guatemala is described as agriculture-driven, a top global exporter of coffee and bananas, with tourism and manufacturing playing supporting roles, but the country still struggles with deep inequality, corruption, and heavy reliance on the US as its top trade partner.

The video closes on culture and food: literature running from the Popol Vuh to Nobel laureate Miguel Angel Asturias, vibrant Mayan weaving and painting, marimba music, and signature dishes like tamales, tostadas, pache de pollo, and jocon that mix Mayan and Spanish influences.

receipts.title: Mayan civilization's classic-period peak
receipts.detail: Between 250 and 900 AD the Mayans built major city-states like Tikal, El Mirador and Kaminaljuyu, with stone pyramids, temples and ball courts, marking the height of their civilization.

receipts.title: Mayan writing and the Popol Vuh
receipts.detail: The Mayans developed a complex hieroglyphic writing system, producing texts including the Popol Vuh creation story, a foundation of Guatemalan cultural identity.

receipts.title: Mayan math used the concept of zero
receipts.detail: Mayan mathematics included the concept of zero and large numbers, part of broader advances in astronomy and calendar systems.

receipts.title: Spanish conquest erased Mayan texts
receipts.detail: After arriving in the early 1500s, the Spanish conquered the Mayans, destroyed many of their texts, and forced conversion to Christianity, provoking some uprisings.

receipts.title: Independence took until 1839 to stick
receipts.detail: Guatemala declared independence in 1821 but passed through the first Mexican Empire and the Federal Republic of Central America before becoming fully independent in 1839.

receipts.title: US-backed coup ended a democratic decade
receipts.detail: A democratic government ruled from 1945 to 1954 until a US-backed coup toppled it, setting off 36 years of civil war.

receipts.title: Civil war targeted indigenous Mayans
receipts.detail: During the 36-year civil war between leftist rebels and military regimes, indigenous Mayans were specifically targeted by the military before the war ended in 1996.

receipts.title: Guatemala is a top coffee and banana exporter
receipts.detail: With a roughly $95 billion GDP and a predominantly agricultural economy, Guatemala ranks among the world's largest exporters of both coffee and bananas.

receipts.title: Poverty persists despite middle-income status
receipts.detail: Guatemala's GDP per capita is around $8,200, technically middle-income, but over 50% of the population lives below the poverty line amid corruption and low tax revenue.

receipts.title: The US dominates Guatemala's trade
receipts.detail: The United States accounts for over a third of Guatemala's exports and a quarter of its imports, making it by far the top trading partner.

receipts.title: Asturias won the Nobel Prize in literature
receipts.detail: Twentieth-century author Miguel Angel Asturias won the Nobel Prize in literature, while Luis Cardoza y Aragon became known for blending surrealism with Mayan myths.
